### 2.1 Kaggle Game Arena — Chess (kaggle-game-arena)

`data/benchmarks/games-planning/kaggle-game-arena.yaml` · `verification_status: ai-drafted-unverified` · curator confidence medium · added 2026-10-04 · last verified 2026-10-04

*Language models play each other at chess, all against all, and are rated by the results.*

A chess benchmark for language models from Google DeepMind and Kaggle. Every pair of models plays 40 games, 20 with each colour, under FIDE rules; each turn the model receives the position and the move history as text and must return one legal move, with three retries before an illegal move loses the game. Ratings are Elo-scaled Bradley-Terry fits to all the pairwise results, anchored so the lowest-rated model is 0, so a rating only means something inside its pool at its date. A second mode, Chess Opening, starts every game from one of 20 popular openings. Models are reached through public APIs at their providers' default settings.

### 2.2 Hanabi Challenge (hanabi)

`data/benchmarks/games-planning/hanabi.yaml` · `verification_status: ai-drafted-unverified` · curator confidence medium · added 2026-10-14 · last verified 2026-10-14

*Cooperative imperfect-information card play for 2-5 agents, scored 0-25 in self-play and with unfamiliar teammates.*

A challenge built on the card game Hanabi, from DeepMind and Google Brain, with an open-source environment, the Hanabi Learning Environment. Two to five players cooperate to build five colour stacks from 1 to 5; each sees every hand but their own, and can tell a teammate about their cards only through hints that name one colour or rank and cost an information token. The team scores a point per card stacked, 25 at most, or nothing if it loses three lives. The paper proposes two challenges. In self-play one learning process controls every seat, in a sample-limited regime of 100 million environment steps or an unlimited one, and the mean score of the best run is reported over at least 1000 games per player count. In ad-hoc team play an agent joins teammates drawn from a held-out pool it has never met, after watching ten of their self-play games. Baselines are learned agents (Rainbow, an IMPALA-based actor-critic, the Bayesian Action Decoder) beside hand-coded bots, which beat the learners in most settings at release. The repository is archived; later work also runs Hanabi in reimplementations such as JaxMARL's.

**Evidence** (33 quoted fields), by checklist area:

#### hanabi · Identity and id

- `self_description` · [S1][hanabi-s1]
  > proposing the game of Hanabi as a new challenge domain with novel problems that arise from its combination of purely cooperative gameplay with two to five players and imperfect information
- `released` = 2019-02-01 · [S1][hanabi-s1]
  > Submitted on 1 Feb 2019

#### hanabi · Domain and capabilities

- `domain` = primary games-planning/card-imperfect-information · [S2][hanabi-s2]
  - why: Hanabi is a card game in which each player sees the others' hands but not their own, so every player holds information the holder of those cards lacks; the paper sets it beside poker rather than chess or Go for that reason.
  > It is also an imperfect information game, where players have asymmetric knowledge about the environment state
- `capability` = collaboration · [S1][hanabi-s1]
  - why: Two to five players share one score, the cards the team stacks together, with no opposed objective anywhere in the game.
  > its combination of purely cooperative gameplay with two to five players and imperfect information
- `capability` = distribution-shift-generalization · [S2][hanabi-s2]
  - why: The ad-hoc challenge scores an agent with teammates from a held-out pool it never trained with, reported as a setting of its own beside self-play. The game and its score are unchanged and only the partners move, which the term's inclusion test sends here rather than to transfer-learning; Melting Pot's classification reads unfamiliar co-players the same way.
  > This is measured via the score achieved by the agent when it is paired with teammates chosen from a held-out pool of agents
- `capability` = sample-efficiency · [S2][hanabi-s2]
  - why: The self-play challenge's sample-limited regime caps training at 100 million environment steps and scores the agent at that budget. The unlimited regime has no cap, so in self-play the term holds for that regime only; ad-hoc play scores the agent after ten of its partners' self-play games (subsets).
  > we propose to limit the number of environment steps that the agent can experience to be at most 100 million
- `evaluation_method` = simulation-rollout · [S2][hanabi-s2]
  - why: Every number is a mean game score over games played in the environment, and each game is scored on a bounded scale, 0 to 25 points.
  > the group scores one point for each card in each stack, for a maximum of 25; otherwise, the score is 0
- `designed_for_subjects` = rl-policy, classical-algorithm · [S4][hanabi-s4]
  - why: The environment is built for policies trained in it, under the two training regimes, and ships a lower-level interface for non-learned methods such as search. The release paper scores hand-coded bots (SmartBot, FireFlower, HatBot, WTFWThat) in the same self-play table as the learners, which classical-algorithm's inclusion test admits as baselines.
  > A lower level game interface is provided in pyhanabi.py for non-RL methods like Monte Carlo tree search.

Considered and rejected:

- `domain` not `games-planning/multi-agent-social` · [S1][hanabi-s1]
  - why: The paper's theme is reasoning about teammates' beliefs and intentions, but the leaf's examples are alliance, betrayal and persuasion, the dynamics of players whose interests can diverge. Hanabi is purely cooperative with a fixed team and no channel but hints, so there is no one to betray or persuade (see review\_checks).
  > its combination of purely cooperative gameplay with two to five players and imperfect information
- `capability` not `long-horizon-execution` · [S2][hanabi-s2]
  - why: A game runs to dozens of dependent turns, and losing three lives or discarding the last copy of a card caps the score, but the default observation hands each agent the card knowledge from past hints, so it need not retain state it generated itself, which the definition asks.
  > This removes the memory task from the challenge
- `capability` not `memory-retention` · [S2][hanabi-s2]
  - why: The minimal observation, without remembered card knowledge, is offered as an option for researchers interested in memory; the challenge's protocol uses the default observation.
  > For researchers interested in memory, we provide the option to request a minimal observation
- `evaluation_method` not `episodic-return` · [S3][hanabi-s3]
  - why: The environment's per-turn rewards sum to the game score, but the term needs a metric with no defined maximum, and its exclusion test removes a return bounded by a maximum that cannot be exceeded. Hanabi's is 25 points, and a 2026 paper notes that not every deal can reach it.
  > Note that the highest return one can achieve in one episode of Hanabi is 25, and one cannot achieve that return in every episode.
- `designed_for_subjects` not `multi-agent-system` · [S2][hanabi-s2]
  - why: In self-play one learning process controls every seat and its joint policy is the entrant, with parameters shared across players in the release baselines; in ad-hoc play the entrant is one agent and its teammates come from a pool the evaluator supplies, which the term's exclusion test treats as environment (see review\_checks).
  > In this case, the learning process is in control of all players, and the objective is to maximise the expected utility of the resulting joint policy

**Open review checks** (10):

1. (field `evaluation_method`) The assignment named episodic-return for the game score. The score is bounded at 25, which episodic-return's tests exclude and simulation-rollout's include, so the entry takes simulation-rollout (simulation profile). Confirm. · [S2][hanabi-s2]
   > the group scores one point for each card in each stack, for a maximum of 25; otherwise, the score is 0
2. (field `domain`) multi-agent-social was rejected because the leaf's examples (alliance, betrayal, persuasion) are dynamics of diverging interests and Hanabi is purely cooperative. If theory-of-mind reasoning about teammates counts as social dynamics, add it as secondary. The vocabulary has no capability for theory of mind, the paper's central claim.
3. (field `capability`) distribution-shift-generalization rests on reading unfamiliar teammates as shifted inputs to an unchanged task, as Melting Pot's classification does; sample-efficiency holds for the sample-limited regime only. Both are set per subset with capability\_override, so the validator's two subset-drops-terms warnings are this deliberate split; confirm it.
4. (field `designed_for_subjects`) multi-agent-system was rejected (a self-play entrant is one joint policy, an ad-hoc entrant one agent with evaluator-supplied teammates); Melting Pot's classification tags it for a focal population scored jointly, which self-play resembles.
5. (field `evaluation_target`) evaluation\_target is learned-system with the hand-coded bots as baselines, following WeatherBench 2 and Open Problems; mixed was considered, since the bots led most of the release table.
6. (field `governance.independence_flags`) maintainer-competes-on-own-benchmark rests on the release paper's own learners (ACHA, and BAD by six of its authors), as RoboCasa's flag rests on its baseline rows; NLE records no flag for its release baselines. · [S2][hanabi-s2]
   > \[38\] J. N. Foerster, F. Song, E. Hughes, N. Burch, I. Dunning, S. Whiteson, M. Botvinick, M. Bowling, Bayesian action decoder for deep multi-agent reinforcement learning
7. (field `lifecycle`) lifecycle active rests on a 2026 paper that runs JaxMARL's reimplementation, not the archived Hanabi Learning Environment. Whether results on a port count as use of the instrument the entry names, and whether they compare with results on the original (the scoring of lost games and the observation must match). · [S3][hanabi-s3]
   > We run experiments in the JaxMARL \[25\] implementations of the popular Hanabi \[4\] and Overcooked \[6\] environments
8. (field `data.contamination_risk`) contamination\_risk medium rests on the ad-hoc pool being the evaluator's choice and possibly public; self-play alone would be low.
9. Identity. The 2018 IEEE CIG Hanabi competition (Mirror and Mixed tracks, scoring lost games by cards played) and later Hanabi challenges, such as the 2025 Ad-Hoc Human-AI Coordination Challenge (seen in a search result, not read), are separate events or entries, not folded in here. · [S2][hanabi-s2]
   > Recently, there was a Hanabi competition that took place at the 2018 IEEE Computational Intelligence in Games Conference in Maastricht
10. (field `data.refresh`) data.refresh is null because the commit history could not be read; a reader with the history should set static or versioned-releases.

### 2.3 Atari 100k (atari-100k)

`data/benchmarks/games-planning/atari-100k.yaml` · `verification_status: ai-drafted-unverified` · curator confidence medium · added 2026-10-14 · last verified 2026-10-14

*26 Atari 2600 games, each learned from scratch in 100k agent steps (400k frames), scored by human-normalised score.*

A sample-efficiency protocol for reinforcement learning on the Arcade Learning Environment (ALE), introduced with SimPLe (arXiv 1903.00374, ICLR 2020). An agent learns each of 26 Atari 2600 games from scratch within 100k agent steps; every action is repeated for 4 frames, so the budget is 400k frames, about two hours of play. The 26 games are those on which SimPLe or a tuned Rainbow reached non-random scores at that budget. A run's score on a game is its return averaged over evaluation episodes after training, normalised so that a random agent scores 0 and an average human 1, and most papers report 3 or 5 runs per game, aggregated across games as the mean and the median. The rliable paper (arXiv 2108.13264, NeurIPS 2021) showed that such point estimates mislead at these run counts and recommended the interquartile mean (IQM) over all runs with stratified bootstrap confidence intervals, which later papers report beside the mean and median. SimPLe's main results ran without sticky actions; the ALE's v5 environments repeat the previous action with probability 0.25 by default and its v4 environments never do, so the environment settings are part of a result. There is no maintainer, site or leaderboard: papers run the protocol and publish their own numbers.

It is a third party's reporting recommendation (no maintainer exists to issue a version), and the per-run, per-game scores it aggregates are unchanged. If the catalogue treats it as a scoring revision, versions would gain a 2019 SimPLe protocol and a 2021 rliable protocol, and refresh would become versioned-releases. The rliable library computes the IQM that papers now report. · [S6][atari-100k-s6]

Results on different settings are not comparable; the simulator\_version condition has to carry it. · [S7][atari-100k-s7]

(field `governance.independence_flags`) The 26 games were chosen by the originators' own results (SimPLe or Rainbow non-random at 100k), which the independence flag rests on together with SimPLe ranking itself in the defining paper. ### 2.4 VideoGameBench (videogamebench)

`data/benchmarks/games-planning/videogamebench.yaml` · `verification_status: ai-drafted-unverified` · curator confidence medium · added 2026-11-09 · last verified 2026-11-18

*VLM agents play 1990s Game Boy and MS-DOS games in real time from raw frames, scored by share of each game completed.*

A benchmark of 23 video games from the 1990s, Game Boy, Game Boy Color and MS-DOS titles run in emulators (PyBoy for Game Boy, JS-DOS in a browser driven by Playwright for MS-DOS), split into a 13-game dev set and a 10-game test set. Seven test games are public (Doom II, Pokemon Crystal, Zelda: Link's Awakening DX, Civilization, The Need for Speed, Kirby's Dream Land DX and The Incredible Machine) and three are secret, held on the maintainers' private evaluation server. A vision-language agent sees only the raw game screen and a short description of the game's objectives and controls; no overlays, game-state access, hints or intermediate rewards are allowed, and actions are key presses, button presses and mouse moves written in language. The task is to complete each game. Progress is tracked automatically: checkpoint frames scraped from YouTube longplay walkthroughs are matched to the emulator's frames by perceptual image hashing, and a game's score is the share of the walkthrough's running time at which the furthest checkpoint reached appears; the overall score averages the games. The game runs in real time, so a model's inference latency costs it; VideoGameBench Lite pauses the emulator while the agent thinks, turning play into turns. In the paper, run with the maintainers' ReAct-style VG-Agent once per game, the best models complete 0.48% of the test set and 1.6% of the Lite test games. Three practice games (clicking, dragging, 2D navigation) probe the interface skills.

  > Therefore, we do not permit any visual overlays, and also do not permit providing any extra information to the agent sourced either from the internal game-state or from the viewable screen.
- `capability` = planning · [S1][videogamebench-s1]
  - why: Each run is played against an explicit objective, completing the game, and the score is how far the executed action sequence got; the source claims planning for the games, which the term's tie-break for interactive episodes needs.
  > also require significant planning (e.g. navigating the world in The Legend of Zelda
- `capability` = spatial-reasoning · [S1][videogamebench-s1]
  - why: Movement and aiming depend on where things are relative to the controlled character or the cursor, inferred from the frame rather than read off, with mouse coordinates on a 640 by 400 screen in the MS-DOS games.
  > controller D-Pad (the flat, four-way directional button on a controller) movement requires understanding positions relative to the game character
- `capability` = memory-retention · [S1][videogamebench-s1]
  - why: What the agent needs (objectives, places visited, items held) is often off-screen by the time it matters, so it must be carried across steps; the paper's failures include agents overwriting their scratchpad and forgetting the objective.
  > Because the games in VideoGameBench require context that is often not visible on-screen
- `capability` = long-horizon-execution · [S1][videogamebench-s1]
  - why: A game runs to thousands of dependent actions, and the paper reports errors that end a run's progress (wasting all ammunition, locking or quitting the emulator); partial credit by checkpoint does not remove the term, whose test is whether full success stays reachable.
  > incorrectly processing the given input frames frequently leads to illogical behavior that can fatally compromise the run
- `evaluation_method` = simulation-rollout · [S1][videogamebench-s1]
  - why: Every number is the outcome of runs in a game emulator, scored per game as the percentage of the game completed by the furthest checkpoint, bounded at 100% (a finished game), and averaged over the games. The scale is bounded, so headroom is defined, and the leading score of 0.48% leaves almost all of it.
  > we track the furthest checkpoint reached by the agent, lookup the timestamp in the associated walkthrough video, and compute the percentage of the game completed
- `designed_for_subjects` = agent-scaffold, model-in-benchmark-harness · [S1][videogamebench-s1]
  - why: Two views, as the taxonomy's model-in-benchmark-harness test allows. The rules constrain inputs and forbid overlays and tools but leave the agent loop to the entrant, the dev set exists to improve models or scaffolds, and the paper's prompts are a starting point entrants may change (agent-scaffold). Every result read runs the maintainers' own VG-Agent with the same prompts, frames and settings, so only the model varies and the leaderboard rows name VG-Agent with the model (model-in-benchmark-harness).
  > These prompts also serve as a starting point for future agents on VideoGameBench, and can be modified if they fall within the rules.

Considered and rejected:

- `domain` not `general-intelligence/novel-task-acquisition` · [S1][videogamebench-s1]
  - why: The family's exclusion test sends a benchmark whose own claim is acquiring tasks it was not built for, with games as the vehicle, to general-intelligence, and the secret games are framed that way. But the headline claim is completing well-known games, the agent is told each game's objectives and controls, seven of the ten test games are public with their prompts, and the secret games are three columns of one average, so the claim is competence at video games and the game family stays primary (see review\_checks).
  > Our objective is not to measure whether agents can play specific games, but whether they can adapt to, learn from, and progress in new environments.
- `capability` not `distribution-shift-generalization` · [S1][videogamebench-s1]
  - why: The secret games are unseen, but they are different games with different objectives, not the same task on shifted inputs, which the term's exclusion test sends to transfer-learning; and their scores are folded into the overall average, not reported as a condition of their own.
  > We keep three of the games secret to encourage solutions that generalize to unseen environments.
- `capability` not `transfer-learning` · [S1][videogamebench-s1]
  - why: A dev set is provided for tuning agents without the test games, which is a move to new environments, but no score of the transfer is reported (the paper reports no dev-set scores and tunes no agent on the dev set).
  > We explicitly provide a dev set to encourage improving the performance of models or minimal scaffolds on interactive environments without using the test set games.
- `evaluation_method` not `episodic-return` · [S1][videogamebench-s1]
  - why: The games give no reward signal and the score is not cumulative reward; it is a completion percentage with 100% as its maximum, which the term's exclusion test removes.
  > we do not provide the agent with any intermediate rewards or signals throughout gameplay

- `reproducible_by_third_party` = false · [S1][videogamebench-s1]

- `task` = exists true; input the raw game screen at each step (in the paper, one frame half a second after each action, or five frames 0.1 seconds apart for MS-DOS games in Lite), with a prompt giving the game's objectives and controls; no overlays, game state or hints; output Actions in language at every step, key presses, held keys, mouse moves, clicks and drags for MS-DOS games, button presses for Game Boy games, while the game runs in real time (or paused while the agent thinks, in Lite), until the run ends.; scoring Per game, the furthest checkpoint reached, detected by a Hamming-distance threshold on perceptual hashes of frames, mapped to the percentage of the walkthrough's running time at which it appears (100% for a finished game); the overall score is the mean over the games. **Open review checks** (11):

1. (field `domain`) The family boundary. Section 2.4 states the aim as adapting to new environments, which is general-intelligence's claim when games are the vehicle. The entry keeps games-planning primary because the headline claim is completing known games, objectives and controls are given, and the three secret games are columns in one average; if the reviewer reads the secret-game aim as the benchmark's claim, primary becomes general-intelligence/novel-task-acquisition with video-games secondary. · [S1][videogamebench-s1]
   > Our objective is not to measure whether agents can play specific games, but whether they can adapt to, learn from, and progress in new environments.
2. (field `task.scoring`) The two scoring descriptions disagree. Section 2.2 says each game is divided uniformly by its checkpoints, but Section 2.6, Table 5 and every published score use the walkthrough-timestamp percentage (Kirby's first of eight checkpoints is 4.81%, not 12.5%). The entry records the timestamp rule. · [S1][videogamebench-s1]
   > Each game is weighted equally (out of 1) and is divided uniformly by the number of predefined checkpoints on each game.
3. (field `learned_entrant_evidence`) Results disagree across versions. The v1 abstract names Gemini 2.5 Pro alone as best at 0.48%; v3 adds Claude 3.7 Sonnet at 0.48% (4.8% on Kirby); the site's leaderboard still shows Sonnet 3.7 at 0% on every game. No source says why the Sonnet score changed. Claims taken from the site and from v3 will conflict. · [S5][videogamebench-s5]
   > VG-Agent + Sonnet 3.7 (claude-3-7-sonnet-20250219) 0% 0% 0% 0% 0% 0% 0%
4. (field `subsets`) VideoGameBench Lite is a subset, as a parallel setting of the same release by the same maintainers scored separately (04 S4). Its set has six games but its headline only the three test games; whether Lite should be a lineage variant instead, or its dev games a child subset, is a reviewer call. · [S1][videogamebench-s1]
   > The list of VideoGameBench Lite games is: Quake, Prince of Persia, Super Mario Land from the dev set, and Doom II, Kirby
5. (field `versions`) The research preview is recorded as a version (revision, breaking) because its game set, split and scoring differ; it published no scores, so it could instead be dropped and noted under released. Its date (April 2025) sits beside the authors' names in the post and is not quoted, so released is null. · [S6][videogamebench-s6]
   > a suite of 20 different popular video games from both hand-held consoles and PC
6. (field `lifecycle`) lifecycle active rests thinly. The only 2026 use found is Rank-Then-Act, which trains a policy on Kirby up to the first checkpoint and reports no VideoGameBench score; 37 citing papers were listed (Semantic Scholar API) and 12 searched for the name, all citing it as related work. No system after the paper's seven has a test-split score in the sources read. null with a log entry is the alternative. · [S3][videogamebench-s3]
   > corresponding to the first checkpoint in VideoGameBench \[31\]
7. (field `activity`) activity accepting-submissions and sandboxed-rerun rest on one README sentence from May 2025. The site gives no submission route and the leaderboard has no outside row; unknown, or no-submission-channel with maintainer-run only, are the alternatives. · S4
   > There are three secret games in the test set which we do not release in this repo. We will run them on our side for new submissions.
8. (field `data.ceiling_anchor_type`) measured-ceiling rests on human playthroughs to completion outside the benchmark's interface; through the interface the authors beat only first checkpoints, and the secret games' walkthroughs are not listed. theoretical-maximum (100%, unchecked through the interface) is the alternative. · [S1][videogamebench-s1]
   > the authors manually beat the first checkpoint of Kirby
9. (field `comparability`) Real-time scores depend on the serving latency of the model, which the paper calls the main limitation; the vocabulary has no capability for acting under a real-time clock and no conditions field for latency (logged with bench tag-gap). Comparisons across providers or dates in real time are not like for like. · [S1][videogamebench-s1]
   > We find inference latency to be a major limitation of frontier models in the real-time setting
10. (field `comparability`) The paper runs each model once per game and its variance check covers three games with Gemini 2.5 Pro; n\_samples of 1 is the protocol as published, which leaves single runs on long games. · [S1][videogamebench-s1]
   > Due to budget constraints, we limit each model to one run on each game.
11. (field `curation.sources`) The site, the research-preview post and the README are withheld from archiving (author names, personal homepages and a personal-account repository). The maintainer field names no individual.

### 2.5 StarCraft Multi-Agent Challenge (smac)

`data/benchmarks/games-planning/smac.yaml` · `verification_status: ai-drafted-unverified` · curator confidence medium · added 2026-11-09 · last verified 2026-11-09

*Decentralised StarCraft II micromanagement battles against the built-in AI, scored by test win rate per map.*

A cooperative multi-agent reinforcement learning benchmark from the University of Oxford's WhiRL lab, built on StarCraft II through Blizzard's machine-learning API and PySC2. Each scenario is a battle between two armies on a fixed map: every allied unit is controlled by its own learned agent, which acts only on observations within its sight range, while the enemy army is played by the game's hand-coded built-in AI at difficulty level 7 ("very difficult"). An episode is won when every enemy unit dies, and lost when the allies die or the time limit runs out. The goal is to maximise the win rate. Training may be centralised, using the global state, but execution must be decentralised. The paper proposes 14 challenge scenarios (the repository lists 23 maps), grouped by the release results into Easy, Hard and Super Hard, and recommends reporting the median test win rate over independent runs, measured with 32 greedy test episodes at intervals during training. PyMARL, the maintainers' training framework, shipped beside it with QMIX, COMA, VDN, IQL and QTRAN. Scores depend on the StarCraft II binary: the README warns that results under SC2 4.10 are not comparable with the paper's 4.6.2. SMACv2 (2022), from the same group, replaces the fixed scenarios with procedurally generated ones.

#### smac · Domain and capabilities

- `domain` = primary games-planning/real-time-strategy · [S1][smac-s1]
  - why: Every scenario is a battle in StarCraft II, a real-time strategy game, in which a team of units must be controlled at once, each by its own agent. The benchmark takes the game's micromanagement component only, not the full game's economy and base-building (see review\_checks on the real-time clause).
  > focuses on micromanagement challenges where each unit is controlled by an independent agent that must act based on local observations
- `capability` = collaboration · [S2][smac-s2]
  - why: All allied agents share one objective, winning the battle, and the score is the team's win rate; the opposing army is the game's scripted AI, not a party the team works with.
  > teams of agents must learn to coordinate their behaviour while conditioning only on their private observations
- `evaluation_method` = simulation-rollout · [S2][smac-s2]
  - why: Every number is a win rate over episodes played in the StarCraft II engine, each episode a win or a loss, so the score is bounded at 100%. The term's inclusion test asks for the simulator and its build to be recorded, which matters here because the SC2 version changes the score.
  > The goal is to maximise the win rate, i.e., the ratio of games won to games played.
- `designed_for_subjects` = rl-policy, multi-agent-system, classical-algorithm · [S2][smac-s2]
  - why: The environment is built for decentralised policies trained in it, one agent per unit, by multi-agent learning algorithms, which the maintainers' PyMARL framework implements. Each unit's agent acts on its own observations and the team's joint behaviour is scored, which multi-agent-system's inclusion test admits. The paper's Table 2 scores a hand-coded focus-fire heuristic beside the learners, which classical-algorithm's inclusion test admits as a baseline.
  > We also plot the performance of a simple heuristic AI that selects the closest enemy unit (ignoring partial observability)

Considered and rejected:

- `domain` not `games-planning/video-games` · [S2][smac-s2]
  - why: StarCraft II is a video game, but SMAC plays it through the raw API's feature vectors and unit-level commands, not the game's ordinary observation and action interface, which the leaf's definition asks for.
  > SMAC uses the raw API of SC2LE.
- `capability` not `communication` · [S2][smac-s2]
  - why: There is no channel between agents at test time; each acts on its own observation history, and the score is the joint outcome, which the term's exclusion test removes.
  > during testing each agent must base its policy solely on its own action-observation history
- `capability` not `sample-efficiency` · [S2][smac-s2]
  - why: The metric is read as a function of environment steps and the paper asks that the steps used be reported, but no budget is fixed and scored at, which the term's exclusion test requires.
  > Our main evaluation metric is the mean win percentage of evaluation episodes as a function of environment steps observed
- `capability` not `distribution-shift-generalization` · [S3][smac-s3]
  - why: The scenarios are fixed, with the same units and start positions in training and test; the SMACv2 paper names this as the gap its procedurally generated scenarios close. It belongs to SMACv2, not to this entry.
  > we show that an open-loop policy, which conditions only on the timestep and ignores all other observations, performs well on many SMAC scenarios
- `evaluation_method` not `episodic-return` · [S2][smac-s2]
  - why: The environment's default shaped reward accumulates over an episode, but it trains the agents and is not the reported metric. The score is a win or a loss per episode, which the term's exclusion test removes; headroom is therefore defined, and the entry can saturate.
  > The percentage of episodes where the agents defeat all enemy units within the permitted time limit is referred to as the test win rate.
- `evaluation_method` not `tournament-play` · [S4][smac-s4]
  - why: Entrants never play each other. Every entrant fights the same built-in AI at a fixed difficulty, a fixed baseline, which the term's exclusion test removes; comparability needs no rating pool.
  > The difficulty of the game AI is set to \_very difficult\_ (7).

The paper runs 32 test episodes every 10,000 training steps over independent runs (five in the paper) and reports the median with the 25-75% percentiles; Table 2 gives the maximum median over the last 250k steps of training.; metric_range 0, 100 · [S2][smac-s2]

**Open review checks** (10):

1. (field `lineage`) Identity (04 S4). SMACv2 is recorded as a same-maintainer variant, a separate Benchmark, not as a version of this entry, and the call is not clear-cut. For a version: the same lab and organisation, the same API and task (decentralised micromanagement against the built-in AI, scored by win rate), the abstract page calls it "a new version of the benchmark" and its README "an update". For a separate entry: its own repository, package and paper (cited separately), new procedurally generated scenarios in place of SMAC's maps, old maps no longer running in it, and the v2 PDF's abstract calling it "a new benchmark". If it were folded in, it would be a version with version\_kind edition and breaking true. · [S3][smac-s3]
   > we introduce SMACv2, a new benchmark where scenarios are procedurally generated and require agents to generalise to previously unseen settings during evaluation
2. (field `domain`) Primary is real-time-strategy, whose definition asks for many simultaneous decisions under real-time pressure. SMAC has the simultaneous decisions (one agent per unit) and is built on an RTS game, but the environment is stepped through the API, so there is no wall-clock pressure on the agents. video-games is the alternative if the clause is read strictly.
3. (field `designed_for_subjects`) multi-agent-system is tagged beside rl-policy, as Melting Pot's entry does for a population scored jointly. Hanabi's entry rejects it because one learning process controls every seat; SMAC's release baselines also share parameters across agents, but each agent acts on its own local observations at test time.
4. (field `governance.independence_flags`) The maintainer-competes-on-own-benchmark flag rests on the release table being the maintainers' own runs in their own framework, as Hanabi's rests on its release learners. That QMIX, the best performer, is by several of the SMAC authors is visible only in the paper's reference list, which this entry does not quote because it names individuals; a reviewer may confirm it.
5. (field `subsets`) The Easy and Super Hard memberships come from the paper's Figures 4 and 6 and Table 2 (the five maps at 97% or more for QMIX, and the five where all methods stay low), not from a sentence; only the Hard four are named in the text. A reviewer with the figures should confirm.
6. (field `aggregation_policy`) aggregation\_policy is official-aggregate on the paper's Figure 3, the median win rate averaged across the 14 scenarios. The methodology section and users (such as arXiv 2605.01805, which averages over its own six maps) report per map; community-aggregate or unknown are the alternatives.
7. (field `lifecycle`) lifecycle active rests on a May 2026 paper using five SMAC maps. The SMACv2 paper argues SMAC no longer rewards algorithmic improvement and the README points to SMACv2, which could support superseded; saturated is derived and not hand-set. The entry states the saturation claim only as the SMACv2 paper does (governance.known\_limitation). · [S3][smac-s3]
   > Recent work reports near-perfect win rates on most scenarios \[55, 13\]
8. (field `data.refresh`) data.refresh is versioned-releases on two releases whose maps are identical; the paper's v5 says its challenge list changed from an earlier version (which arXiv version is not stated), and later commits are not tagged (GitHub API, read 2026-11-09). The commit history was not read for changes to scenarios or scoring; static is the alternative if none exist.
9. (field `execution.reproducibility_blockers`) The StarCraft II binary is a proprietary dependency. Blizzard's terms for the Linux builds and the game were not read, so no licence-restriction blocker is recorded; the specific-simulator-build blocker rests on the README's warning that SC2 versions are not comparable.
10. (field `release_venue`) The task framing named AAMAS 2019 (extended abstract) as a venue; no source read states it. release\_venue is the NeurIPS 2019 Deep RL workshop from the v5 PDF's first page.

**Reviewer checklist** for `smac`:

- [ ] Identity and id: the name, aliases, id, paper and release date are right, and this is one benchmark, not a family or an edition of another
- [ ] Domain and capabilities: the primary and secondary subdomains, capabilities, evaluation methods and intended subjects fit, and no rejected term should have been kept
- [ ] Task and evaluation: the task, scoring, ground truth, entrants and harness read as the sources describe them
- [ ] Data and licence: access, refresh, provenance, sizes, subsets, contamination and licences match the sources
- [ ] Governance and independence: maintainer type, submission process, funding and independence flags are right
- [ ] Lifecycle and activity: lifecycle, activity, versions, editions and history are current
- [ ] Every open review check above is answered or resolved
- [ ] Nothing here would embarrass the catalogue in front of a specialist

### 2.6 Craftax (craftax)

`data/benchmarks/games-planning/craftax.yaml` · `verification_status: ai-drafted-unverified` · curator confidence medium · added 2026-10-14 · last verified 2026-10-14

*Open-ended RL in JAX: an extended Crafter, scored by achievements unlocked within a fixed budget of environment steps.*

An open-ended reinforcement-learning environment written in JAX. Craftax-Classic rewrites Crafter, a 2D survival game like a simplified Minecraft, with 22 achievements. Craftax, the main environment, extends it with mechanics inspired by NetHack: nine procedurally generated floors, from caves and dungeons to a boss floor, 19 creatures, ranged and magic combat, potions whose effects are permuted every episode, and 65 achievements. The agent is rewarded the first time it completes each achievement in an episode, with harder categories worth more (1, 3, 5 or 8), and loses or regains 0.1 per point of health; results are reported as a percentage of the maximum reward, 226. The paper proposes two benchmarks on the symbolic observations: Craftax-1B, a budget of one billion environment interactions, and Craftax-1M, one million, as a test of sample efficiency. Because the whole pipeline compiles to the GPU, a 1B run takes about an hour on one GPU. The baselines (PPO, PPO with a recurrent network, and exploration bonuses) reach 11-15% of the maximum on Craftax-1B. A scoreboard in the README takes further results by pull request, unverified.

#### craftax · Domain and capabilities

- `domain` = primary games-planning/open-ended-environments · [S1][craftax-s1]
  - why: An agent acts in a game world with no single goal, and the score is the achievements it unlocks, which is the leaf's definition; the family's own example names Craftax for open-ended achievement progression.
  > giving the agent a reward the first time each achievement is completed each episode
- `capability` = search-exploration · [S1][craftax-s1]
  - why: The reward is discovery itself, the first completion of each achievement in an episode, under a fixed budget of environment interactions; the paper presents the benchmark as a hard exploration task and evaluates exploration methods on it.
  > Craftax assesses deep exploration whereas XLand-Minigrid assesses wide generalisation
- `capability` = long-horizon-execution · [S1][craftax-s1]
  - why: An episode runs to thousands of dependent actions, and the player's death ends it, so an early error makes the remaining achievements unattainable in that episode.
  > successful runs typically take tens of thousands of frames
- `capability` = planning · [S1][craftax-s1]
  - why: Each episode is played against an explicit objective, the weighted achievements, and the source claims long-term planning, so the executed action sequence is the plan and its reward scores it (the term's tie-break for interactive episodes).
  > Solving Craftax requires deep exploration, long term planning and memory, as well as continual adaptation to novel situations as more of the world is discovered
- `capability` = memory-retention · [S1][craftax-s1]
  - why: Potion effects are permuted every episode, so an effect found by trial must be kept across the intervening steps until a potion is next used; the paper names memory as what this tests.
  > an agent will need to discover which potions correspond to which effects through trial and error each episode, further testing in-context learning and memory
- `capability` = sample-efficiency · [S1][craftax-s1]
  - why: Both benchmarks fix a budget of environment interactions and score the reward reached at it; Craftax-1M is proposed as a sample-efficiency test outright, while Craftax-1B's budget is set high on purpose.

1. (field `domain`) Primary is open-ended-environments, as the family's example has it, but homographs.yaml calls Craftax a procedural-generalization entry. The paper scores on in-distribution levels with no held-out set, so procedural-generalization was rejected even as secondary; it could come back as secondary on the paper's hope of generalisation across generated worlds. · [S1][craftax-s1]

2. (field `capability`) The taxonomy's examples tag Craftax with continual-learning, compositional-generalization, creativity-novelty and self-improvement; each fails its own inclusion test on the sources read and is rejected with the reason. Either the examples or this entry should change.
3. (field `designed_for_subjects`) rl-policy is tagged although its own example calls Craftax a near miss for prompted language agents. Every result read is a trained policy; no source read shows a language agent on Craftax, so observed\_subjects is left empty.
4. (field `data.ceiling_anchor_type`) measured-ceiling rests on one author's perfect run in one world, in a GUI with unlimited time per move; whether that establishes 226 as reachable across worlds, or the anchor is theoretical-maximum, is a judgement. · [S1][craftax-s1]

5. (field `data.access`) data.access is generated-on-demand here, where nle.yaml has fully-open for the same situation (worlds generated from seeds); the family's two entries should agree.

(field `governance.independence_flags`) maintainer-competes-on-own-benchmark rests on the maintainers' baseline rows on the scoreboard, as robocasa's flag does; whether baselines of standard algorithms count. The README's request for "a reference to the source of the results" was not read as publication-gated.
7. (field `lineage`) Multi-Agent Craftax (arXiv 2511.04904) was not read; it is a separate entry or an extension recorded in lineage.

### 2.7 Procgen Benchmark (procgen)

`data/benchmarks/games-planning/procgen.yaml` · `verification_status: ai-drafted-unverified` · curator confidence medium · added 2026-11-09 · last verified 2026-11-09

*16 procedurally generated 2D games for RL: train on 500 levels, score on unseen ones, or train and test on all.*

A suite of 16 procedurally generated game-like environments for reinforcement learning, released by OpenAI in December 2019 and published at ICML 2020. Each environment (BigFish, BossFight, CaveFlyer, Chaser, Climber, CoinRun, Dodgeball, FruitBot, Heist, Jumper, Leaper, Maze, Miner, Ninja, Plunder, StarPilot) generates its level layout, assets, entity placement and spawn times from a level seed, and all share 64x64 RGB observations and a 15-action discrete space. The paper defines two protocols. For generalization, an agent trains on a finite set of levels, 500 in the default hard mode or 200 in the easy mode, and is scored zero-shot on the full distribution of levels; for sample efficiency it trains and is tested on the full distribution. The reference budget is 200M environment steps in hard mode (about 24 GPU-hours with the paper's PPO per environment) and 25M in easy mode, which needs about an eighth of the compute. Scores are mean episodic return per environment; a single score across the suite is the mean normalised return, (R - Rmin)/(Rmax - Rmin) with published per-environment constants, which almost always falls between 0 and 1. Baselines are PPO and Rainbow with the IMPALA convolutional network. Some environments also offer memory and exploration modes, which are not part of the two protocols. The environments run on CPU, install from PyPI, and are kept in their released form, known bugs included, so that published results stay reproducible; the README marks the repository as in maintenance. There is no leaderboard: papers run the protocols and report their own numbers.

#### procgen · Domain and capabilities

- `domain` = primary games-planning/procedural-generalization; secondary games-planning/video-games · [S2][procgen-s2]
  - why: An agent plays episodes against environments that respond, and the headline protocol trains on a finite set of procedurally generated levels and scores on levels it has not seen, which is the leaf's definition. The games mimic Atari and Gym Retro titles and are played from pixels through a button-combination action space, which is the secondary leaf.
  > zero-shot performance averaged over unseen levels
- `capability` = compositional-generalization · [S2][procgen-s2]
  - why: The game mechanics and asset pools are fixed per environment and the generator recombines them per level; the paper enumerates for each environment what generation controls (counts, types and positions of platforms, obstacles, enemies), and held-out levels are new arrangements of those. The taxonomy names procgen as the term's example.
  > Procedural generation controls the number of platform sections, their corresponding types, the location of crates, and the location and types of obstacles
- `capability` = sample-efficiency · [S2][procgen-s2]
  - why: The sample-efficiency protocol trains and tests on the full level distribution under a fixed reference budget, 200M steps in hard mode and 25M in easy, and reports return over that budget; the abstract names sample efficiency as one of the two things measured.
  > training for 200M timesteps with PPO on a single Procgen environment requires approximately 24 GPU-hrs and 60 CPU-hrs
- `evaluation_method` = episodic-return · [S2][procgen-s2]
  - why: Per environment, the reported number is mean raw episodic return. The suite-level score rescales it with constants "chosen to approximately bound R", so a normalised return can pass 1; for StarPilot and FruitBot Rmax is the score a long PPO run reached, not a bound. The term's exclusion test keeps a reference constant that agents can exceed as episodic-return, so headroom is undefined (see review\_checks).
  > We report the mean raw episodic return, where each episode includes a single level
- `designed_for_subjects` = rl-policy · [S2][procgen-s2]
  - why: The environments are built to train and evaluate reinforcement-learning policies, and every result read is a trained policy (PPO and Rainbow in the paper, PPO in arXiv 2609.32532).
  > PPO performs much more consistently across the benchmark

Considered and rejected:

- `capability` not `distribution-shift-generalization` · [S2][procgen-s2]
  - why: Test levels come from the same generator as training levels and differ by the seed only, a difference by random sampling that the term's exclusion test removes; the taxonomy names procgen as its near miss.
  > we use a training set of 500 levels to evaluate generalization in each environment
- `capability` not `perception` · [S2][procgen-s2]
  - why: The paper says success depends on recognising assets in the pixels, but the score is the game's return, not what was recovered from the images; atari-100k rejects it the same way.
  > Performing well primarily depends on identifying critical assets in the observation space
- `capability` not `memory-retention` · [S2][procgen-s2]
  - why: The default environments need little memory, and the memory variants are a separate distribution mode that neither protocol uses.
  > By default, Procgen environments require little to no use of memory
- `capability` not `search-exploration` · [S2][procgen-s2]
  - why: Eight environments can be run as hard-exploration tasks on a single hand-picked level, but that setting is outside both protocols and measures no generalisation.
  > We note that generalization is not measured in this setting
- `evaluation_method` not `simulation-rollout` · [S2][procgen-s2]
  - why: Episodes run in a simulator, but the reported quantity is cumulative return, and the normalisation constants only approximately bound it; for eleven environments Rmax is the theoretical maximum, which would argue for a bounded method on those alone.
  > the normalized return will almost always fall between 0 and 1

1. (field `evaluation_method`) evaluation\_method is episodic-return, so headroom is null, as the brief directs. But for 11 of the 16 environments Rmax is the theoretical and practical maximum, and for 3 more an average of the best achievable reward, so most per-environment normalised returns cannot exceed about 1; only StarPilot's and FruitBot's Rmax is a score an agent can beat. Whether the suite should be a bounded method (simulation-rollout, as craftax is) or per-subset metrics is a reviewer call. · [S2][procgen-s2]
   > the maximal theoretical and practical reward is trivial to compute
2. (field `data.ceiling_anchor_type`) ceiling\_anchor\_type is null because Rmax mixes three kinds of anchor. measured-ceiling fits the five environments with empirical Rmax, theoretical-maximum the other eleven; ceiling\_by\_category could carry them per environment if a single value is wanted. · [S2][procgen-s2]
   > Rmax in these environments as the score PPO achieves after 8 billion timesteps
3. (field `capability`) compositional-generalization follows the taxonomy's own example, on the per-environment lists of what generation controls. Generation also picks assets and backgrounds from pools, a change in input statistics closer to distribution shift; whether every primitive in a test level was seen in 500 training levels is not stated. · [S2][procgen-s2]
   > Procedural generation logic governs the level layout
4. (field `domain`) video-games is secondary on the pixel observations and button-combo actions a human can also play with (procgen.interactive). craftax rejected video-games for a game built as an RL environment; Procgen's games are also built for RL, so the two entries should agree. · [S4][procgen-s4]
   > The expected step rate for a human player is 15 Hz.
5. (field `activity`) The README names a 2020 competition (NeurIPS 2020, on AIcrowd) on these environments. It was not read and is not folded in, as nle.yaml does with the NetHack Challenge; if the catalogue records it as an event here, activity becomes closed with a history entry. · [S4][procgen-s4]
   > We ran a competition in 2020 which used these environments to measure sample efficiency and generalization in RL.
6. (field `versions`) No versions are recorded. The package had 12 releases from 0.9.1 (2019-12-03) to 0.10.7 (2022-01-24) by GitHub's release record, which was read but is not a Source; the README says the environments are kept as released. 0.10.0 changed the info dictionary and added flags; whether any release changed level generation was not checked against the code.
7. (field `lifecycle`) The README's status line (Maintenance) is recorded only in lifecycle\_basis, since maintenance\_status is derived; the repository's last push (2026-03-27) pinned workflow references, by its commit message, and was not checked for environment changes. · [S4][procgen-s4]
   > Maintenance (expect bug fixes and minor updates)
8. (field `subsets`) The paper says 6 of the 16 environments have memory variants but lists seven names; the README lists memory and exploration as game-specific distribution modes. Neither mode is in the two protocols, so no subset is recorded for them. · [S2][procgen-s2]
   > evaluation of memory are CoinRun, CaveFlyer, Dodgeball, Miner, Jumper, Maze, and Heist
9. (field `lifecycle`) The evidence of current use is a single-author preprint that is not peer reviewed and runs an 8M-step budget rather than the paper's 25M; a peer-reviewed 2025-2026 paper (for example Impoola, RLC 2025, arXiv 2503.05546, seen in an arXiv listing and not read) would be a firmer anchor for lifecycle.

(field `curation.sources`) The announcement page and the paper name the authors and, on the page, many people in the acknowledgements; the windows keep clear of them, and contains\_personal\_data is false on both Sources. The page was read from a Wayback capture because openai.com answered 403 (robots.txt allows it).

### 2.8 Melting Pot (melting-pot)

`data/benchmarks/games-planning/melting-pot.yaml` · `verification_status: ai-drafted-unverified` · curator confidence medium · added 2026-10-14 · last verified 2026-10-14

*Multi-agent RL suite scoring trained populations against unfamiliar co-players in 256+ held-out social scenarios.*

A multi-agent reinforcement learning evaluation suite from DeepMind, built on the DeepMind Lab2D gridworld engine. A substrate is a partially observed multi-agent game, from social dilemmas such as Clean Up and Commons Harvest to coordination games, matrix games played in space and team competitions such as Paintball. A test scenario pairs a substrate with a background population of pretrained bots that the agents under test have never met. The entrant is a multi-agent population learning algorithm: it may train a population on the substrates however it likes, and the population is then placed zero-shot into the scenarios, in resident mode (focal players in the majority) or visitor mode (background bots in the majority). The primary metric is the focal-population per-capita return, the mean return of the focal players; the release papers min-max normalise it per scenario between the worst and best agent evaluated and average it over each substrate's scenarios. Melting Pot 1.0 (ICML 2021) had 21 substrates and over 80 scenarios; Melting Pot 2.0 (2022) replaced them all, added roles for asymmetric games, and the suite now counts over 50 substrates and over 256 scenarios. A NeurIPS 2023 contest on AIcrowd, run with the Cooperative AI Foundation and MIT, scored submitted populations on held-out scenarios of four substrates; those scenarios joined the package in v2.3.0. There is no standing leaderboard, and results appear in users' papers.

### 2.9 BALROG (balrog)

`data/benchmarks/games-planning/balrog.yaml` · `verification_status: ai-drafted-unverified` · curator confidence medium · added 2026-11-09 · last verified 2026-11-09

*LLMs and VLMs play six existing RL games through one text harness, scored by average progress from 0 to 100.*

A benchmark and evaluation framework for LLMs and VLMs as agents in long-horizon games, from a group spanning UCL's AI Centre, IDEAS NCBR, Oxford, NYU and Warsaw. It wraps six existing reinforcement-learning environments of rising difficulty: BabyAI (five grid-world navigation tasks set in natural language), Crafter (a 2D survival and crafting game), TextWorld (three text adventures), Baba Is AI (40 rule-rewriting puzzles after Baba Is You), MiniHack (maze, corridor, combat, Sokoban-like and quest tasks built on NetHack) and NetHack itself through the NetHack Learning Environment. Each step, the model receives the game's rules and actions, then the recent observation-action history as text (16 observations in the paper), plus an image of the current state in VLM mode, and must return one action in natural language; an invalid action is reported back and replaced by a default. Each episode scores 0 to 100: success or failure in BabyAI, Baba Is AI and MiniHack, the share of achievements in Crafter and TextWorld, and in NetHack a new progression measure built from human games (the probability of eventually winning from the deepest dungeon or highest experience level reached). The headline % Progress averages the environments. Because every environment is procedurally generated, episodes are not stored. The paper's zero-shot baselines run in the framework's own naive agent, led by Claude 3.5 Sonnet at 32.64% language-only; the leaderboard takes submissions by pull request, with optional verification, and its LLM board is led at 68.3% (September 2026), where NetHack progress is still at most 13.2%.

#### balrog · Domain and capabilities

- `domain` = primary games-planning/multi-game-suites; secondary games-planning/puzzle-games, games-planning/open-ended-environments, games-planning/video-games · [S2][balrog-s2]
  - why: Every score comes from episodes against a responding game environment, and the suite spans several of the family's subdomains with none holding most of it, Baba Is AI a puzzle game, Crafter an open-ended achievement game and NetHack a roguelike video game, averaged into one progress score; the paper's claim is breadth across games.
  > Specifically BALROG enables seamless running of LLM and VLM agents on BabyAI, Crafter, TextWorld, Baba Is AI, MiniHack, and NetHack
- `capability` = planning · [S2][balrog-s2]
  - why: Each episode is played against an explicit goal (a mission, the achievements, the win condition or the stairs down), and the source claims long-term planning, so the executed action sequence is the plan and its progress scores it (the term's tie-break for interactive episodes).
  > It supports model evaluation on challenging reinforcement learning environments that test skills such as long-term planning, spatial reasoning, and the ability to deduce the mechanics of the environment.
- `capability` = long-horizon-execution · [S2][balrog-s2]
  - why: Episodes run from tens of steps (BabyAI) to tens of thousands (NetHack) of dependent actions with environment feedback between them, and dying or an irreversible move (a boulder pushed into a corner) makes full success on the episode unattainable; partial credit in Crafter, TextWorld and NetHack does not disqualify it.
  > while all of these games are long-horizon, they span a broad range of difficulty levels
- `capability` = spatial-reasoning · [S4][balrog-s4]
  - why: Every environment has a navigation component, and progress depends on positions and layouts the agent must infer from relative descriptions ("a wall 5 steps forward") or an image; the site repeats the claim. The taxonomy names BALROG as the term's example.
  > testing their ability to plan, reason spatially, and explore in dynamic environments
- `evaluation_method` = simulation-rollout · [S2][balrog-s2]
  - why: Every number is the outcome of episodes run in the environments' simulators, each scored on a bounded 0-100 scale, success or failure in three environments and the share of achievements or progression in the other three, so one term carries both; the per-environment formulas are in task.scoring.
  > For environments like MiniHack, BabyAI, and Baba Is AI, each episode is scored as either 0 or 100 based on task completion.
- `designed_for_subjects` = model-in-benchmark-harness, agent-scaffold · [S2][balrog-s2]
  - why: The leaderboard takes two kinds of entry. A new model is evaluated zero-shot inside BALROG's own naive agent, the same prompts and loop for every entrant, which the taxonomy names as model-in-benchmark-harness's example; an agentic strategy replaces that loop (agent.py) with the entrant's own prompting or reasoning method around an existing model.
  > Submissions may propose novel inference-time prompting strategies for improving the reasoning, planning, or in-context learning capability of an existing model.

Considered and rejected:

- `domain` not `games-planning/procedural-generalization` · [S2][balrog-s2]
  - why: All six environments are procedurally generated, but the protocol is zero-shot, with no training levels and no held-out split; the paper presents the generation as a guard against memorisation and leakage, not as a measure of generalisation to unseen levels (review\_checks).
  > all of the environments used in the benchmark are procedurally generated, and encountering the same instance of an environment twice is unlikely
- `domain` not `general-intelligence/agi-composite-suites` · [S2][balrog-s2]
  - why: The paper hopes to spur generalist agents and averages heterogeneous tasks into one score, but its breadth lies inside one family, games, which general-intelligence's exclusion test sends to that family's suite leaf.
  > we look to spur progress on developing truly generalist agents
- `capability` not `search-exploration` · [S2][balrog-s2]
  - why: The site and the paper claim exploration, and Crafter's milestones reward discovery, but the headline averages task completion and progress; nothing scores how the space was traversed, and Crafter is one environment of six.
  > Agents are evaluated based on the number of achieved milestones, such as discovering new resources and crafting tools
- `capability` not `instruction-following` · [S2][balrog-s2]
  - why: The paper says models must read the rules and produce valid actions, but invalid actions are replaced by a default rather than scored, and the source claims agentic capability, not instruction following.
  > BALROG provides feedback to the agent indicating the action
- `capability` not `perception` · [S2][balrog-s2]
  - why: The VLM track adds an image of the current state, but the score is game progress, and the paper reports that images mostly lower it rather than measuring what was recovered from them.
  > we find that multimodal LLMs perform much worse when also presented with an image of the environment rather than a textual-only description of the observation
- `evaluation_method` not `episodic-return` · [S2][balrog-s2]
  - why: NetHack's own in-game score accumulates without bound, but BALROG replaces it with a progression measure that runs from 0 at the start of the game to 100 at ascension, so no environment's score is unbounded; the term's exclusion test sends it to a bounded method.
  > and ascension as 100% progression
- `designed_for_subjects` not `instruction-tuned-model` · [S2][balrog-s2]
  - why: The model is prompted at every step of a multi-turn loop with environment feedback, not once, which the term's exclusion test sends to model-in-benchmark-harness.
  > By default, these models will be evaluated zero-shot.

**Open review checks** (10):

1. (field `governance.independence_flags`) The independence flags are not assessed. The paper thanks the Gemini Academic Program for support of unstated kind and Gemini models are ranked; if a reviewer confirms the programme is the model provider's and the support was money, credits or compute, funded-by-evaluated-party applies (the Stage 3 record set it). One author's Anthropic affiliation, with Claude models ranked, has no flag of its own.
2. (field `subsets`) Stage 3's record says the leaderboard has LLM, VLM and Agent modes. The page read has two tabs, LLM and VLM; Agent is the heading of the model column. Subsets follow the page. · [S4][balrog-s4]
   > Agent % Progress BabyAI Crafter BabaIsAI MiniHack NetHack Date
3. (field `governance.submission_process`) The site's legend for the check mark speaks of reproducing "the patch generations", which reads as copied from SWE-bench's template (the site says it uses it); the submission page's own wording is a re-run on a random subset. The five September 2026 rows, the board's top three among them, are unverified. · [S4][balrog-s4]
   > Checked indicates that we, the BALROG team, received access to the system and were able to reproduce the patch generations.
4. (field `external_ids.epoch`) Epoch's string "Balrog" names no track. Its score column, Average progress, matches both boards' headline; which board (LLM or VLM) Epoch reads was not checked against its CSV rows. · [S1][balrog-s1]
   > Balrog,True,balrog\_external.csv,Average progress
5. (field `versions`) No versions are recorded. The board mixes rows from 2024-11 to 2026-09 run on whatever harness commit the entrant used, with history length, temperature and agent left to the entrant, and BALROG labels no release; the paper's v1 and v2 are revisions of the text, not of the benchmark. If the harness or the environment wrappers changed scoring, a revision belongs here.
6. (field `domain`) procedural-generalization was rejected. All environments are procedurally generated and the models never trained on them, which could be read as evaluation on unseen levels; the paper presents the generation as leakage control and has no train/test split. · [S2][balrog-s2]
   > ensuring rigorous and fair comparisons by preventing test-set leakage
7. (field `data.access`) data.access is generated-on-demand, as craftax has it, where nle.yaml has fully-open for the same situation. No source read says whether evaluation seeds are fixed, which decides whether two runs see the same episodes.
8. (field `data.size`) The paper's MiniHack task list differs between section 2.1 (five tasks) and Appendix E (Maze 9x9 and 15x15, Corridor, CorridorBattle, Quest Easy and Medium, Boxoban), and the episode count per task is not stated; data.size follows section 2.1. · [S2][balrog-s2]
   > From the MiniHack Navigation Tasks, we picked Maze 9x9, Maze 15x15, Corridor and CorridorBattle
9. (field `subsets`) The domain overrides on the Crafter, Baba Is AI and NetHack subsets, and the secondaries, are drawn from the paper's descriptions of the environments; BabyAI, TextWorld and MiniHack get none because no single leaf fits them. A reviewer may prefer no overrides.
10. (field `observed_subjects`) The newest rows carry a Max suffix (GPT-6-Astra-Max, Claude-Opus-5-Max) whose meaning, presumably a reasoning-effort setting, no source read states; the experiments repository's metadata for them was not read.

### 2.10 TextArena (textarena)

`data/benchmarks/games-planning/textarena.yaml` · `verification_status: ai-drafted-unverified` · curator confidence medium · added 2026-11-09 · last verified 2026-11-09

*Language-model agents play 100+ text games against each other and people, rated by TrueSkill on a live leaderboard.*

An open-source collection of text-based games for evaluating and training language-model agents, with a Gym-style interface (an agent is any function from a text observation to a text action) and an online leaderboard. The games are single-player puzzles (Sudoku, Wordle, Minesweeper), two-player board, card and word games (chess, Othello, Kuhn poker, Taboo), negotiation and social dilemmas, and multi-player social-deduction and bargaining games (Secret Mafia, Codenames, Diplomacy). The paper launched with 57 games and counted 74 at publication; the README now says over 100, with interfaces in 192 languages. Online, entrants play each other and human players through the maintainers' matchmaking server, and each is rated with TrueSkill per environment and per environment grouping (the default view is a seven-game Balanced Subset); humans share one rating, Humanity. The maintainers host many commercial models themselves, and anyone may enter an agent. When read on 2026-11-09 every row of the board was marked inactive. The NeurIPS 2025 MindGames competition ran four of its games on the same server.

#### textarena · Identity and id

#### textarena · Domain and capabilities

- `domain` = primary games-planning/multi-game-suites; secondary games-planning/board-games, games-planning/card-imperfect-information, games-planning/puzzle-games, reasoning-general/theory-of-mind · [S2][textarena-s2]
  - why: The games span several of the family's subdomains -- interactive single-player puzzles, perfect-information board games, card and dice games with hidden information, and negotiation and social-deduction games -- and the paper's appendix lists them by player count, not by one kind. Its claim is breadth across capabilities within games, which the term's inclusion test asks; the subdomains go secondary, multi-agent-social apart (rejected below). reasoning-general/theory-of-mind is secondary because the paper names theory of mind first among the skills its games test.
  > These games test a wide range of capabilities, including theory of mind, persuasion, deception, spatial reasoning, long-term planning and other social skills that traditional benchmarks typically do not assess.
- `capability` = planning · [S2][textarena-s2]
  - why: Each game is an interactive episode against an explicit objective, winning, so the executed moves are the plan and the game's outcome scores it, and the source claims planning: long-term planning among the capabilities the games test, and Strategic Planning the most common of the soft skills the paper tags its games with.
  > These games test a wide range of capabilities, including theory of mind, persuasion, deception, spatial reasoning, long-term planning and other social skills that traditional benchmarks typically do not assess.
- `evaluation_method` = tournament-play · [S2][textarena-s2]
  - why: Entrants play each other, and human players, in the maintainers' online system, and the result is a TrueSkill rating fitted to those games, per environment and per grouping -- tournament-play's inclusion test. The paper chose TrueSkill because it handles games with more than two players.
  > The online competition system facilitates both Model vs Model and Model vs Human play across our diverse library of environments.
- `designed_for_subjects` = agent-scaffold, model-in-benchmark-harness · [S2][textarena-s2]
  - why: Two kinds of entrant are rated side by side. Community entrants bring their own agent, any function from observation to action with whatever prompting or loop it contains (agent-scaffold; the README's interface, and MindGames' winners relied on explicit scaffolding). The maintainers also host official models, listed under provider model names and played by the platform itself, so for those rows only the model varies inside the maintainers' wrapper (model-in-benchmark-harness). No source read states the hosted models' prompt or wrapper.
  > So far, we have evaluated 283 models online, including community submissions and the 64 official models hosted by the platform.

Considered and rejected:

- `domain` not `games-planning/multi-agent-social` · [S2][textarena-s2]
  - why: The abstract foregrounds social skills, and the multi-player list is mostly social deduction and bargaining. But the appendix's single-player list is all puzzles and most of its two-player list is board, card, dice and word games, so social dynamics do not hold most of the games. It is the runner-up for primary, and since a term cannot be both assigned and rejected it is not listed as secondary either; the social games are carried by reasoning-general/theory-of-mind.
  > Traditional benchmarks rarely assess dynamic social skills such as negotiation, theory of mind, and deception
- `evaluation_method` not `pairwise-preference-elo` · [S2][textarena-s2]
  - why: The paper sets itself against Chatbot Arena's votes; outcomes here are played games, and the term's exclusion test removes direct play.
  > humans select which of two LLM-generated answers they prefer

The pool also moves (live-world-state).

#### textarena · Data and licence

- `data.access` = generated-on-demand · [S2][textarena-s2]
  - why: The scored items are games, produced afresh in every match by entrants playing each other in the game engines -- the term's own case. There is no item set to obtain; the environments themselves are open.
  > TextArena facilitates offline model development/training and online competition between models and human players (both model vs model and model vs human)
- `data.refresh` = rolling-live · [S2][textarena-s2]
  - why: The game collection grows without labelled versions -- 57 at launch, 74 at publication, over 100 in the README -- and the rating pool changes as entrants come and go, so a rating needs its date and grouping to be read.
  > As of publication, the collection has grown to 74 games and continues to expand.
- `data.data_provenance` = synthetic-procedural · [S2][textarena-s2]
  > Importantly, all games used are either naively text-based or adapted to be text-based.
- `data.ceiling_anchor_type` = none-known · [S2][textarena-s2]
  - why: The paper chose a relative rating so that there is no top end; a TrueSkill mean has no maximum, and Humanity's rating is one entrant in the pool, not a ceiling scores are read against.
  > The advantage thereof is that there is no clear upper limit of performance that can be reached
- `data.size` = count 100; unit games; subset the repository at commit 1e3160d · [S5][textarena-s5]
  > A suite of 100+ single-, two-, and multi-player text-based games for benchmarking and training LLMs.

  > The resulting harness prevents all illegal moves in 145 different TextArena games (both 1-player and 2-player)
- `data.size` = count 74; unit games; subset the paper's v2 (16 single-player, 47 two-player, 11 multi-player) · [S2][textarena-s2]
  > As of publication, the collection has grown to 74 games and continues to expand.

#### textarena · Lifecycle and activity

- `lifecycle` = active · [S3][textarena-s3]
  - why: Results are still produced on the games. AutoHarness (February 2026) ran Gemini-2.5-Flash with synthesised harnesses on 145 TextArena games, and MindGames' 2025 competition rated 944 submitted agents on four. The online board itself showed no active model on 2026-11-09 (activity).

- `activity` = unknown · [S4][textarena-s4]
  - why: The submission route still exists in the code at the pinned commit (ta.make\_online and an example script), but whether the online board takes entries now could not be established. Every row the leaderboard loaded on 2026-11-09, for the Balanced Subset and for all environments, was marked inactive, which on the page's own rule means fewer than 5 games in the last 14 days; and the matchmaking server the client connects to did not answer an HTTPS request that day (a timeout, not quoted). accepting-submissions would need the route to be open now.
  > For most environments, inactivity means playing fewer than 5 games in the last 14 days.
- `events` = name MindGames, NeurIPS 2025 competition (Stage I and II on the TextArena online leaderboard); kind online-challenge · [S4][textarena-s4]

**Open review checks** (10):

1. (field `comparability.rating_pool_required`) No data/rating-pools/ record and no subsets. The leaderboard's rows and its groupings (a default Balanced Subset, an All grouping and skill groupings) load from a database endpoint whose request carries a privileged key shipped in the site's script, so they are not cited. A pool record (rating\_system trueskill) and the groupings as subsets wait on a public export or archivable page that lists them.
2. (field `activity`) activity unknown. The code keeps the online route, but every leaderboard row was inactive on 2026-11-09 and the matchmaking host timed out. A reviewer who can see a game being played, or a statement that the server is closed, should set accepting-submissions or closed. · [S7][textarena-s7]
   > env = ta.make\_online(
3. (field `domain.primary`) multi-game-suites against multi-agent-social. The abstract's own claim is social skills, and the corpus has no classification record for TextArena. The call rests on the appendix's game lists; no count by subdomain was computed (05 S4). Rejecting multi-agent-social as primary also keeps it out of secondary, though social-deduction and bargaining games are a large part of the suite; a reviewer may prefer it secondary, with this check carrying the rejection. · [S1][textarena-s1]
   > allows for easy evaluation of model capabilities via an online-play system (against humans and other submitted models) with real-time TrueSkill scores
4. (field `governance.independence_flags`) funded-by-evaluated-party rests on an acknowledgement of support "in various capacities" from Anthropic, whose models are rated; if the support was not money, credits or compute, the flag should go. OpenRouter and AWS are thanked too; whether their own systems are rated was not checked.
5. (field `designed_for_subjects`) model-in-benchmark-harness for the hosted official models rests on the paper's "hosted by the platform"; no source read gives their prompt or wrapper, or says the same wrapper is used for all of them.
6. (field `governance.maintainer_type`) maintainer\_type community-collective. The paper's first affiliation is A\*STAR's Centre for Frontier AI Research; if A\*STAR holds the project, the type is academic-lab or government-agency.
7. (field `lineage`) MindGames as a variant, not a fork. Same server and the README's "we", but its own organiser team, GitHub organisation, site and dataset. If the lead judges it separately maintained, it becomes a fork with that team as maintainer. · [S5][textarena-s5]
   > We released the findings of
8. (field `versions`) No versions are modelled. The collection grows game by game with no tags or GitHub releases (API, 2026-11-09), environments carry their own -v0 ids, and the README dates package releases (v0.6.9 with 100 games, July 2025). Whether those package releases should be editions under 04 S4 is not clear-cut; PyPI's release history was not read (its robots.txt disallows the JSON API).
9. (field `capability`) theory of mind, persuasion and deception, the skills the paper says set it apart, have no capability term; logged with bench tag-gap.
10. (field `repository`) The paper and README link the repository under its earlier personal-account home; the canonical repository is now the TextArena organisation (GitHub API). No history event is recorded because no source read dates the move.

**Reviewer checklist** for `textarena`:

- [ ] Identity and id: the name, aliases, id, paper and release date are right, and this is one benchmark, not a family or an edition of another
- [ ] Domain and capabilities: the primary and secondary subdomains, capabilities, evaluation methods and intended subjects fit, and no rejected term should have been kept
- [ ] Task and evaluation: the task, scoring, ground truth, entrants and harness read as the sources describe them
- [ ] Data and licence: access, refresh, provenance, sizes, subsets, contamination and licences match the sources
- [ ] Governance and independence: maintainer type, submission process, funding and independence flags are right
- [ ] Lifecycle and activity: lifecycle, activity, versions, editions and history are current
- [ ] Every open review check above is answered or resolved
- [ ] Nothing here would embarrass the catalogue in front of a specialist
